chapter.title: Design a Notification System
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Design a scalable notification system that supports mobile push notifications, SMS, and email, delivers notifications as soon as practical, respects user opt-in settings, scales horizontally, avoids data loss, reduces duplicates, retries failures, and supports monitoring and analytics.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 10 designs a multi-channel notification platform for iOS push, Android push, SMS, and email. The interview scope is soft real-time delivery: notifications should arrive as soon as possible, but small delays are acceptable under high load. Notifications may be triggered by client applications or scheduled server-side. The assumed daily scale is 10 million mobile push notifications, 1 million SMS messages, and 5 million emails. The initial architecture places a single notification server between triggering services and third-party delivery providers, but this creates a single point of failure, independent-scaling problems, and performance bottlenecks. The improved design separates database/cache from notification servers, horizontally scales notification servers, and introduces per-channel message queues and worker pools. The deep dive focuses on reliability, durable notification logs, retries, deduplication rather than exactly-once guarantees, templates, user notification settings, rate limiting, push API security, queue monitoring, analytics/event tracking, and an updated end-to-end design.
chapter_summary.central_architectural_idea: Decouple notification ingestion from delivery using message queues and independent workers for each notification type.

real_time_requirement.meaning: Deliver as soon as possible, but slight delay is acceptable when the system is under high workload.

ios_push.provider_role: Builds and sends notification requests to APNS.

request_data.device_token: Unique identifier used for sending push notifications.
request_data.payload: JSON dictionary containing the notification payload.

ios_push.apns_role: Apple remote service that propagates push notifications to iOS devices.

android_push.flow: Similar to iOS push, but Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) is commonly used instead of APNS.

sms.delivery: Usually delegated to third-party commercial SMS services.

email.delivery: Companies may host their own email infrastructure, but many choose commercial services.

contact_information_flow.collection_trigger: When the user installs the app or signs up for the first time.
flow: User installs app or signs up.
Contact information is stored in the database.

database_model.relationship: One user can have multiple devices.

contact_information_flow.implication: A push notification can be sent to all of a user's devices.

triggering_services.name: Service 1 to N
examples: Billing service sends payment-due reminder emails.
Shopping service sends package-delivery SMS notifications.

responsibilities: Build notification payloads for third-party services.

third_party_services.extensibility_requirement: The design should make third-party providers easy to plug in or unplug.
third_party_services.regional_availability_example: FCM is unavailable in China, so alternatives such as Jpush or PushY may be used.

initial_design_problems.reason: A single notification server can take down the notification pipeline if it fails.
Database, cache, and notification-processing responsibilities are coupled inside one server, making independent scaling difficult.
Payload rendering and waiting for third-party responses can be resource-intensive and overload the server during peak periods.

major_changes: Move database and cache out of the notification server.
Add multiple notification servers with automatic horizontal scaling.
Introduce message queues to decouple system components.

services_1_to_n.role: Call notification-server APIs to initiate notifications.

responsibilities: Provide APIs for services to send notifications.
Restrict APIs to internal or verified clients to prevent spam.
Perform basic validation of email addresses, phone numbers, and related data.
Query database/cache for data needed to render notifications.
Place notification data onto message queues for parallel processing.

api_example.source_context: The text introduces this as an example API to send an email.
api_example.source_discrepancy_note: The chapter labels the example as an email API while the printed endpoint path contains '/sms/send'. This guide preserves that discrepancy rather than silently correcting it.

purposes: Act as buffers during high notification volume.
message_queues.per_channel_isolation: Each notification type receives a distinct queue so a failure in one third-party provider does not affect other notification channels.

workers.role: Pull notification events from message queues and send them to the appropriate third-party services.

third_party_services.role: Deliver notifications to final user devices/accounts.

notification_sending_flow.action: An upstream service calls an API exposed by notification servers.
Notification servers fetch metadata such as user information, device token, and notification settings from cache or database.
The notification event is sent to the appropriate channel-specific message queue.
Workers pull notification events from message queues.
Workers send notifications to corresponding third-party services.
Third-party services deliver notifications to user devices/accounts.

data_loss.requirement: Notifications may be delayed or reordered, but should never be lost.
techniques: Persist notification data in a database.
Use a notification log database for persistence.

exactly_once.chapter_statement: Exactly-once delivery cannot be guaranteed in the distributed design; duplicate notifications may occur.
dedupe_strategy: When an event arrives, check its event ID.
If the event ID has already been seen, discard the event.
If it has not been seen, send the notification.
exactly_once.goal: Reduce duplicate occurrence, not provide a strict exactly-once guarantee.

notification_templates.definition: Preformatted notifications customized with parameters, styling, tracking links, and similar fields.

notification_settings.purpose: Give users fine-grained control because excessive notifications can be overwhelming.
notification_settings.send_rule: Check whether the user is opted in for that notification type before sending.

rate_limiting.purpose: Limit how many notifications a user receives so the system does not overwhelm users and cause them to disable notifications entirely.

retry_mechanism.trigger: A third-party provider fails to send a notification.
behavior: Put the notification back into the message queue.
If the failure persists, alert developers.
retry_mechanism.updated_design_detail: The updated design retries a predefined number of times.

push_security.policy: Only authenticated or verified clients may invoke push-notification APIs.

queue_monitoring.interpretation: A large queue indicates workers are not processing notification events quickly enough.
queue_monitoring.response: Add more workers to reduce delivery delay.

event_tracking.integration: Notification system usually integrates with an analytics service.

new_features.behavior: Failed notifications are returned to the messaging queue and retried by workers a predefined number of times.

new_features.purpose: System health checks and future improvements.

major_takeaways: Support push notification, SMS, and email.
Use message queues to decouple system components.
Use retry mechanisms to reduce delivery failures.
Use appKey/appSecret to secure push APIs for verified clients.
Track and monitor key metrics at any stage of the flow.
Respect user opt-out settings before sending.
Use rate limiting/frequency capping to avoid overwhelming users.

key_concepts.definition: Notifications should arrive quickly, but a slight delay is acceptable under high load.
A unique identifier used to send push notifications to a device.
JSON dictionary containing push-notification content and metadata.
Apple Push Notification Service, which delivers push notifications to iOS devices.
Firebase Cloud Messaging, commonly used for Android push notifications.
Single point of failure; the initial design has one notification server whose failure can stop the system.
A buffer that decouples notification ingestion from delivery workers and enables parallel processing.
A server/process that pulls notification events from queues and invokes third-party delivery services.
Persistent storage used to prevent notification data from being lost.
Checking event IDs to discard already-seen notification events and reduce duplicate delivery.
A reusable preformatted notification customized with parameters and styling.
Per-user, per-channel preferences such as opt-in status.
Frequency capping on notifications to avoid overwhelming a user.
Requeueing failed notification events and retrying delivery.
The number of queued notifications, monitored as a signal that workers may be falling behind.
Capturing open rate, click rate, engagement, and other metrics through analytics integration.

short_answer_questions.question: What makes notification-system design more complex than simply calling APNS or an SMS API?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The system must handle multiple channels, user/device metadata, high volume, provider-specific integrations, horizontal scaling, queueing, retries, data durability, duplicate suppression, preferences, rate limits, security, monitoring, and analytics.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the iOS push-notification flow.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A provider constructs a request containing a device token and JSON payload, sends it to APNS, and APNS propagates the notification to the target iOS device.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does the improved architecture use message queues?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Queues decouple notification servers from delivery workers, buffer traffic spikes, enable parallel processing, and isolate channels so a failure in one provider does not stop other notification types.

short_answer_questions.question: What responsibilities remain in the notification servers after the architecture is decomposed?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They expose controlled APIs, validate inputs, fetch user/device/template/settings data from cache or DB, and enqueue notification data into the proper channel queue.

short_answer_questions.question: Why use different message queues for iOS, Android, SMS, and email?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Separate queues provide independent processing and failure isolation. An outage or slowdown in one third-party service does not have to block unrelated channels.

short_answer_questions.question: How does the chapter handle notification reliability?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Persist notification data in a database/notification log so it is not lost, then use retry logic when delivery fails.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is exactly-once delivery not guaranteed?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Distributed failures and retries can cause the same event to be processed more than once. The chapter therefore uses deduplication by event ID to reduce duplicates instead of promising strict exactly-once delivery.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the difference between notification settings and rate limiting?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Settings decide whether a user has opted into a particular channel at all. Rate limiting controls how frequently an opted-in user receives notifications.

short_answer_questions.question: How does the system respond when workers fall behind?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Monitor the number of queued notifications. A large backlog means events are not being processed quickly enough, so more workers should be added.

short_answer_questions.question: What does analytics add to the system?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Analytics event tracking records metrics such as open rate, click rate, and engagement so customer behavior can be understood and the notification system can be improved.

interview_style_questions.question: What requirements would you clarify for a notification system?
How do the delivery mechanisms differ by channel?
Why is the single notification-server design inadequate?

strong_answer_outline: Accept that strict exactly-once is unavailable

strong_answer_outline: Alert developers on persistent provider failures
Use monitoring for health and future improvement

common_confusions.confusion: A notification system is just mobile push.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter explicitly includes push notifications, SMS, and email.

common_confusions.confusion: Soft real-time means arbitrary delays are acceptable.
common_confusions.correction: The goal is still to deliver as soon as possible; only slight delays are acceptable under heavy load.

common_confusions.confusion: APNS is the Android push provider.
common_confusions.correction: APNS is for iOS; FCM is commonly used for Android.

common_confusions.confusion: One user has only one device token.
common_confusions.correction: The schema allows one user to have multiple devices/device tokens.

common_confusions.confusion: One notification server is simpler, so it is sufficient.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter identifies SPOF, scaling, and performance problems and replaces it with horizontally scaled servers and queues.

common_confusions.confusion: One shared queue is always enough for all notification channels.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter gives each notification type a separate queue to isolate third-party outages and processing.
The chapter explicitly says exactly-once delivery is not guaranteed and introduces event-ID deduplication to reduce duplicates.

common_confusions.confusion: Rate limiting is only an infrastructure protection mechanism.
common_confusions.correction: Here it is explicitly used to avoid overwhelming users with too many notifications.

common_confusions.confusion: A large queue is merely a storage issue.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter treats queue depth as an operational signal that workers may be processing too slowly.

common_confusions.confusion: The example API path on page 158 clearly matches the text label.
common_confusions.correction: The source says the example is for sending an email but prints an endpoint containing '/sms/send'; this guide preserves the discrepancy.

practice_problems.prompt: Using the chapter's daily assumptions, how many total notifications are sent per day?
practice_problems.note: Derived directly from the stated channel volumes.

practice_problems.prompt: The SMS provider experiences a two-hour outage. How should the queue architecture prevent push and email from stalling?
practice_problems.solution: Use a distinct SMS queue and SMS workers so the SMS backlog is isolated from iOS, Android, and email queues.

practice_problems.prompt: Event ID E123 was successfully processed, but the same event appears again after a retry race. What should happen?
practice_problems.solution: Detect that E123 has already been seen and discard the repeated event.

practice_problems.prompt: Queue depth rises from 10,000 to 500,000 while ingress rate is stable. What does the chapter's monitoring logic suggest?
practice_problems.solution: Workers are falling behind; add more workers to increase processing throughput.

practice_problems.prompt: A user has opt_in=false for email but opt_in=true for push. Which channel should be suppressed?
practice_problems.solution: Email should be suppressed; push can still be sent subject to other rules.

practice_problems.prompt: Why should notification rendering data such as templates be cached?
practice_problems.solution: The chapter places templates and user/device information in cache so notification servers can fetch frequently needed rendering metadata efficiently.

must_memorize: Channels: push notification, SMS, email.
Soft real-time: deliver ASAP; slight delay is acceptable under heavy load.
Scale: 10M push + 1M SMS + 5M email per day.
iOS push: Provider -> APNS -> device.
Android push: commonly FCM.
SMS examples: Twilio, Nexmo.
Email examples: Sendgrid, Mailchimp.
Collect device tokens, phone numbers, and email addresses at install/sign-up.
One user can have multiple devices.
Initial design problems: SPOF, hard to scale, performance bottleneck.
Improved design: external DB/cache, multiple notification servers, message queues.
Notification server: secure API, validate, fetch metadata, enqueue.
Separate queue per notification type for buffering and failure isolation.
Workers consume queues and call third-party services.
Reliability: persist notification data and retry.
Exactly-once delivery is not guaranteed.
Dedupe using event ID.
Templates improve consistency, reduce errors, and save time.
Check per-channel opt-in before sending.
Rate limit to avoid overwhelming users.
Failed notifications are requeued; persistent failure triggers developer alerts.
Secure push APIs with appKey/appSecret and verified clients.
Monitor queued-notification count; large backlog means add workers.
Track open rate, click rate, and engagement through analytics.
Final design adds authentication, rate limiting, retries, templates, monitoring, and tracking.
chapter_ten_final_review.memory_chain: TRIGGER -> NOTIFICATION SERVER -> CACHE/DB METADATA -> CHANNEL QUEUE -> WORKER -> THIRD-PARTY PROVIDER -> USER || DURABILITY + RETRY + DEDUPE || SETTINGS + RATE LIMIT || AUTH + MONITORING + ANALYTICS
chapter_ten_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: A scalable notification platform separates notification ingestion from channel delivery using durable, channel-specific queues and workers, then adds retries, deduplication, user preferences, rate limiting, security, monitoring, and analytics to make delivery reliable and operable.
